terms.comment: Properly harsh to the taste, of unripe fruit; then of grief, words, people.

evidence: Varr. RR 1.66 (Lewis & Short): not in Cicero or the poets

phrases.latin: Theodōrus olīvam ē catīnō gustāvit, quae jam amāra nōn erat
phrases.english: Theo tasted an olive from the dish, which was no longer bitter
phrases.source: Libellus III, Apud avum et aviam

phrases.english: I don’t want this; it’s bitter.

phrases.latin: ut puerōrum aetās inprōvida lūdificētur labrōrum tenus, intereā perpōtet amārum absinthī laticem dēceptaque nōn capiātur
phrases.english: so that the unwary age of children may be fooled as far as the lips, and meanwhile drink down the bitter juice of wormwood, and be tricked but not harmed

sources: John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 280.

Theodōrus et pater · Ad Larem avītum, Libellī I–VII, as they stood on 7 November 2026, with their glosses. Examples marked “Libellus” quote those texts word for word; classical passages are cited by author.
